recommendations: Run n01 to n07 in outline order, playlist numbers 54 to 60, after t06 (53). Networks and Data analysis are parallel strands; the playlist runs n then d. No split: every design fits under 570 s (about 493 to 501 s estimated).

Joins: n01 opens on t06's final frame exactly (the flight-route map); t06's provisional mark is lifted. Each later video opens on the previous video's final frame. n07 closes the strand ('Networks, paths and trees: done') and hands to math-s11-d01 with a survey phone (provisional until d01 is designed).

Each 'Next' chip quotes the next video's on-screen heading: n01 'Networks'; n02 'Degree, direction and weight'; n03 'Networks from tables and maps'; n04 'Paths, trees and spanning trees'; n05 'Minimum spanning trees'; n06 'Shortest paths'; n07 'When shortest isn't best'; d01 'Statistical investigations' (provisional).

Strand colour roles (fixed n01 to n07): vertices blue; edges and arrows amber; weights white on amber tags; highlighted routes, chosen edges and spanning trees teal; cycles and removed edges violet; a 'best path by another measure' green outline; answer green; mistake red.

Recurring models introduced once: the NetworkBoard (n01; directed and weighted with a runner from n02); the morph with a fixed connection list (n01); the token drop for the degree sum (n02); the table-to-network builder and map straightener (n03); the route lister (n03); the path walker, subgraph overlay and spanning-tree carousel (n04); the MST builder with cycle flashes (n05); the spread race, label table and trace-back (n06); the weight toggle and tree-against-trip overlay (n07). Recurring anchors: the flight map (t06 to n02), the van's town (n01, n02), the rail trail (n02, n03), the camp (n03 to n05, n07), the toll network (n06, n07).

Memory aids introduced once: n01 'Dots for things, lines for links.'; n02 'Degree: count the lines at a dot. Arrows give direction; numbers give weight.'; n03 'Name the vertices, then turn every filled cell into an edge, with its number as the weight.'; n04 'A tree reaches everything and never loops back.'; n05 'Cheapest first. Skip any link that closes a loop. Stop when everything is joined.'; n06 'Label outwards. Lock in the smallest. Update its neighbours.'; n07 'Shortest is about one number. Best is about everything that matters.'

Everyday anchors (no people, hands or faces; no science contexts): flights, a train map, towers, a rail trail, pipes, a delivery run, a social app as account dots (n01); a van's one-way streets (n02); a rail trail and a town's one-way streets (n03); a school camp's lighting (n04); fibre to towers, pipelines (n05); a delivery van, a bus, a cyclist (n06); a toll road, a motorway, floods and hills (n07).
Prices: only n05's example $25,000 per km of fibre (labelled 'example price'). Speeds in n07 (50 and 100 km/h) are examples.

Facts Codex confirms: the 2024 glossary definitions of path, tree, spanning tree and minimum spanning tree (n04); uniqueness of every shortest path and MST used where 'any' or 'the' is claimed (n06, n07); the count of 21 spanning trees (n04); that the method name Dijkstra appears nowhere (n06).
No new plate: every plate used exists and was viewed (delivery van, phone, phone tower, rail trail, hiking valley, country town, country road, bus, share e-bike, road sign post, hillside strip).
Header strip (owner rule of 23 Nov): the focus area only, 'NETWORKS, PATHS AND TREES'.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: What is a network, and where do networks appear in real life?

syllabusActions.text: Describe a network as a collection of objects (vertices) interconnected by lines (edges) that can represent systems in the real world
Examine circumstances in which networks are used in a variety of real-world applications
